questions.question: In policy learning from offline data, what does the generalization error of a learned policy primarily measure?
questions.choice_A: The gap between the policy’s expected return under the population distribution and its empirical estimate from the dataset
questions.choice_B: The difference between training and validation loss for the reward model
questions.choice_C: The number of times the policy chooses the optimal action on the training set
questions.choice_D: The variance of the importance weights alone

questions.question: Which complexity measure is most commonly used to derive uniform convergence bounds for a class of policies in contextual bandits?
questions.choice_A: The raw number of parameters in the policy network
questions.choice_B: Rademacher complexity of the induced loss class (e.g., weighted 0-1 loss)
questions.choice_C: The training objective value at convergence
questions.choice_D: The maximum observed reward in the dataset

questions.question: In off-policy evaluation with logged behavior policy \(\mu(a\mid x)\) and target policy \(\pi(a\mid x)\), which expression gives the per-step importance weight used in inverse propensity scoring?
questions.choice_A: \(w(x,a) = \mu(a\mid x) / \pi(a\mid x)\)
questions.choice_B: \(w(x,a) = \pi(x\mid a) / \mu(x\mid a)\)
questions.choice_C: \(w(x,a) = \pi(a\mid x) / \mu(a\mid x)\)
questions.choice_D: \(w(x,a) = R(x,a) / \mathbb{E}[R]\)

questions.question: Which statement about self-normalized importance sampling (SNIS) for off-policy evaluation is most accurate?
questions.choice_A: SNIS is unbiased and always has lower variance than IPS
questions.choice_B: SNIS is unbiased but can have higher variance than IPS
questions.choice_C: SNIS is biased and inconsistent
questions.choice_D: SNIS is biased at finite samples but consistent; the bias vanishes as sample size grows

questions.question: Which condition is necessary for unbiased off-policy evaluation using importance sampling?
questions.choice_A: Overlap (positivity): if \(\pi(a\mid x) > 0\) then \(\mu(a\mid x) > 0\)
questions.choice_B: The logging policy must be deterministic
questions.choice_C: Rewards must be normally distributed
questions.choice_D: The target policy must be identical to the logging policy

questions.question: Under the Bradley–Terry–Luce model for pairwise preferences, which identifiability/consistency statement is correct for the maximum likelihood estimator?
questions.choice_A: Utilities are identifiable without any constraints and converge to the true values exactly
questions.choice_B: Utilities are identifiable only up to an additive constant, and the MLE is consistent under correct model specification and sufficient comparisons
questions.choice_C: Utilities are identifiable only up to a multiplicative constant, and the MLE is inconsistent
questions.choice_D: Utilities are neither identifiable nor consistently estimable even under the correct model

questions.question: Which description best captures the bias–variance trade-off among standard off-policy estimators?
questions.choice_A: IPS has low variance but high bias; the Direct Method (DM) has high variance but low bias
questions.choice_B: Both IPS and DM are unbiased but have equal variance
questions.choice_C: IPS is unbiased but can have very high variance; DM often has lower variance but can be biased due to model misspecification; Doubly Robust aims to combine the best of both
questions.choice_D: Doubly Robust is unbiased only if both the model and propensities are correct

questions.question: In generalization analyses for off-policy policy learning, what role do concentrability coefficients (or distribution mismatch coefficients) play?
questions.choice_A: They guarantee low variance of all estimators regardless of policy class
questions.choice_B: They measure optimization suboptimality of the policy gradient method
questions.choice_C: They quantify the Lipschitz constant of the reward function
questions.choice_D: They capture how much the target occupancy can be dominated by the data-generating occupancy, scaling the difficulty of generalization

questions.question: What is the main effect of clipping large importance weights at a threshold \(c\) in off-policy evaluation?
questions.choice_A: Introduces bias but can substantially reduce variance and mean squared error
questions.choice_B: Eliminates bias without affecting variance
questions.choice_C: Ensures exact overlap between policies
questions.choice_D: Makes the estimator consistent in smaller sample sizes

questions.question: Consistency of preference-based estimators from pairwise comparisons typically requires which condition?
questions.choice_A: Rewards are bounded in \([0,1]\)
questions.choice_B: The true preference formation process is within the estimator’s model class (e.g., correct link) and comparisons are sufficiently informative
questions.choice_C: All pairs are compared an equal number of times
questions.choice_D: The logging policy is uniformly random over items

questions.question: Which is the defining property of the doubly robust (DR) estimator for off-policy evaluation?
questions.choice_A: It minimizes variance regardless of data size
questions.choice_B: It is unbiased if and only if both the outcome model and propensity model are correct
questions.choice_C: It is unbiased if either the outcome model or the propensity model is correctly specified
questions.choice_D: It never uses importance weights

questions.question: Which approach directly addresses distribution shift between SFT training data and deployment in offline policy optimization?
questions.choice_A: Training a larger reward model without regularization
questions.choice_B: Dropping samples with low propensities
questions.choice_C: Using only on-policy data for evaluation
questions.choice_D: Regularizing the learned policy towards the behavior policy (e.g., KL constraints or trust-region penalties) to limit extrapolation

questions.question: Which factor most commonly inflates generalization error bounds for off-policy policy learning in contextual bandits?
questions.choice_A: Heavy-tailed or large importance weights due to poor overlap
questions.choice_B: High training accuracy of the reward model
questions.choice_C: Low capacity (simple) policy classes
questions.choice_D: Large validation sets

questions.question: Why is off-policy evaluation particularly fragile when the logging policy is deterministic?
questions.choice_A: Because the rewards become heteroscedastic
questions.choice_B: Because actions not chosen by the logging policy have zero propensity, breaking overlap for those actions
questions.choice_C: Because importance weights are always equal to one
questions.choice_D: Because deterministic policies eliminate variance entirely

questions.question: In moderate sample regimes with mild model misspecification, which estimator often achieves the best mean squared error in practice for off-policy evaluation?
questions.choice_A: Inverse Propensity Scoring (IPS)
questions.choice_B: Self-normalized IPS only
questions.choice_C: Doubly Robust (DR)
questions.choice_D: Unweighted sample average of rewards

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of structural risk minimization (SRM) to control policy class complexity in offline policy learning?
questions.choice_A: Choosing the policy that maximizes empirical return without constraints
questions.choice_B: Always using the most expressive model available
questions.choice_C: Ignoring generalization error and optimizing training return only
questions.choice_D: Selecting among a nested sequence of policy classes based on a complexity-penalized criterion or cross-validation

questions.question: What is a primary challenge of off-policy evaluation with continuous action spaces?
questions.choice_A: Estimating stable and accurate density ratios \(\pi(a\mid x)/\mu(a\mid x)\) for continuous \(a\)
questions.choice_B: Lack of any feasible logging policy
questions.choice_C: The impossibility of model-based estimation
questions.choice_D: The absence of distribution shift

questions.question: Which statement best describes a distributionally robust approach to offline policy evaluation or optimization?
questions.choice_A: It assumes the deployment distribution matches the training distribution exactly
questions.choice_B: It optimizes or evaluates worst-case performance over distributions within an \(f\)-divergence ball around the empirical/logging distribution
questions.choice_C: It ignores samples with high importance weights
questions.choice_D: It replaces rewards with their empirical means without any correction

questions.question: For consistency of preference-based utility learning from pairwise comparisons across many items, which graph condition on the comparison data is typically required?
questions.choice_A: Each item must be compared to every other item exactly once
questions.choice_B: The comparison graph must be a complete clique
questions.choice_C: The comparison graph must be strongly connected (or at least connected/ergodic), ensuring information propagation
questions.choice_D: No structural condition is required as long as sample size is large

questions.question: How can control variates (baselines) be used with importance sampling for off-policy evaluation without introducing bias?
questions.choice_A: By subtracting the sample mean reward from each term
questions.choice_B: By reweighting rewards until the weights sum to one
questions.choice_C: By adding any function of context and action to the reward
questions.choice_D: By subtracting a function with zero mean under the logging distribution, preserving unbiasedness while reducing variance
